meta.title: Configure ai-jail: flags, config files, masking and lockdown
meta.description: Every ai-jail capability is off until you turn it on, except your toolchains and the agent's own login. See each flag and config key, how to hide secrets inside a project, what lockdown does, and recipes you can copy.

hero.title: Closed by default. You hold the switches.
hero.lede: With no options, the agent gets your project, your build tools on Linux, its own login and its own API host, and no network beyond that and a short list of package registries. You turn things down one switch at a time, and lockdown closes most of them at once.

authority.title: Three places a setting can come from
authority.lede: Settings come from a file inside the project, a file in your home directory and the flags you type. They are listed from least to most authority.
authority.alt: Three sources feed the jail. The project .ai-jail file can only tighten it. The global ~/.ai-jail file is trusted. Command-line flags win over both. Inside the jail sits the agent behind a row of switches, most of them off.
authority.caption: A repository you cloned cannot open its own jail.

points.title: Project .ai-jail
points.text: ai-jail treats it as untrusted: it can tighten the jail and never open it. ai-jail never follows it through a symlink, and the agent sees an empty file in its place.

points.title: Global ~/.ai-jail
points.text: It is yours, so ai-jail trusts it. It holds a base table for every run, plus [commands.<name>] tables chosen by the first word of the command.

points.title: Command-line flags
points.text: Flags have the highest authority. Most switches come in pairs, such as --network and --no-network, so a flag can also close what a file opened.

authority.merge: In a command table, single values replace the base and lists such as maps and masks are added to it.
authority.codeClaude: # only when the command starts with "claude"

trust.title: When a team ships its own policy
trust.text: List a parent directory under trust_project_config in the global file, and project files beneath it may open capabilities too. Everything under that directory is trusted, including repositories you clone there later, so keep the list narrow.

switches.title: The switches
switches.lede: Every row is off until you ask, except the two cyan rows, which are on by default. Each capability flag has a --no- twin that closes it again. A red badge marks a switch that weakens the jail. Security has the full list and the reasons.

rows.text: The whole network. Anything the agent can read, it can send out. If the agent only needs a few hosts, --allow-host is the tighter choice. Without either flag, the sandbox reaches only the package registries that toolchains open through the proxy, plus the one API host of a known agent (Claude, Codex, Gemini, Grok), and --no-network closes all of those.

The sandbox reaches only the listed host and its subdomains, over TCP through ai-jail's built-in proxy. You can repeat the flag. An explicit list replaces the default, so include the agent's API host yourself. It cannot be combined with --network or --browser, and a project file may only shrink the list.
Your ~/.ssh, read only, and your SSH agent socket, so git push works.
The Docker socket. This is effectively root on your machine, because the daemon can start containers that mount the host.
The Tailscale socket.
The systemd user bus. The agent can ask your user manager to run services on the host. Linux only.

The agent's own login. The invoked harness's state, such as ~/.claude or ~/.codex, is mounted read and write, and its API key is copied from your shell when set: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, MOONSHOT_API_KEY. The agent starts logged in, and anything in the jail can use that login. --no-agent-state gives a logged-out run. Off under lockdown, and a project file can only turn it off.
Uses the given directory as Claude's state and sets CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR.

Passes one variable from your shell, or sets one with NAME=VALUE. Repeatable and never saved to disk. On Linux the values travel to the sandbox through an in-memory file and never appear on the launcher's command line, but a literal NAME=VALUE is still visible on ai-jail's own command line, so for a secret prefer --env NAME or --env-from-file.

Reads strict KEY=VALUE lines from a file and passes them like --env, which wins on conflicts. The file must be yours, a regular file, mode 0600 or stricter, and outside the project, or the launch fails. ai-jail never saves the values to disk, and the config key works from the global file only.

Keeps the real value of KEY out of the sandbox. The agent sees a placeholder, and the proxy puts the real value only into requests to that one host. Needs --allow-host, and the key must already come in through --env or --env-from-file. Global file only, never saved. It covers clients that can talk plain HTTP to the proxy for that host; HTTPS tunnels are untouched.
Passes your whole shell environment, every secret in it included. Avoid it.
The same as --env, from the global file only. A project file that sets it is ignored.

Your compilers and package managers read only, their dependency caches in a store the jail owns, and the package registries reachable through the filtered proxy. Linux only, and on by default there; on macOS nothing is mapped and no registry is reachable. Lockdown turns it off, and a project file can only turn it off. Details below.

Your gh config directory, read only, plus your active github.com token forwarded as GH_TOKEN for that launch, so gh is logged in even when the token lives in the system keyring. ai-jail asks gh auth token on the host and passes the result through an in-memory file, never on a command line or on disk; --dry-run never fetches it, and a GH_TOKEN you pass with --env skips the lookup. Only github.com and only the active account. Anything in the jail can still act as you on GitHub.
Your ~/.aws, read only. Anything in the jail can act as you on AWS while the credential is valid.
Your ~/.kube, read only. Anything in the jail can talk to your clusters as you.
Your ~/.config/gcloud, read only. Anything in the jail can act as you on Google Cloud.
Your ~/.docker/config.json, read only, which holds your registry logins. Anything in the jail can use them.
GPU devices, and with them the driver's attack surface. Linux only.

/dev/kvm, for hardware-accelerated virtual machines such as QEMU or an Android emulator. It exposes the host kernel's KVM interface. Guests get only the sandbox's network, and no tun or vhost devices. Linux only.
The Wayland socket and nothing else from your session. Linux only.
The X11 socket. X11 lets a program log keystrokes and take screenshots.
PipeWire and PulseAudio sockets and /dev/snd. Anything in the jail can record and play audio. Linux only.
The host's /dev/shm, which opens shared memory with processes outside the jail.
Your ~/Pictures, read only.
A separate browser profile. hard (the default) keeps nothing between runs, soft keeps a profile under ~/.local/share/ai-jail/browsers.
Mounts one more path read only. Write SOURCE:DEST to mount it somewhere else. Repeatable.
Mounts one more path read and write. Repeatable.
Mounts a path copy-on-write: the agent's writes go to a side layer and the original stays untouched. Linux only; on macOS it becomes a read-only mount.
Never mounts the named dot-directory, for example .my_secrets. Repeatable.

groups.title: Layers you can turn off, and should not

rows.text: Turns off Landlock, the kernel's own copy of the file rules. Refused under --lockdown.
Turns off the filter that blocks dangerous system calls.
Turns off the limits that stop runaway processes.
Gives up the fresh home directory. This is broad access to your real home. Prefer --map for the one path you need.

Appends one record per launch to ~/.local/share/ai-jail/history.jsonl (directory 0700, file 0600): time, command, effective capabilities, config sources, exit code and duration. With --allow-host, every allowed or denied connection is recorded too, and with --secret, every injection. Each line carries the hash of the one before it. It is off by default, and a project file can turn it off but not on.

Prints a readable summary of the log and exits: launches, filtered-network decisions and secret substitutions. It does not check the chain. Exit 0 after a display, 1 for malformed records or a read error, 2 when there is no log. Launch records can include command arguments, so keep secrets out of them.
Walks the audit log's hash chain and exits: 0 when it is intact, 1 at the first broken link, 2 when there is no log. Records written before 2.2 are reported as legacy, which is not an error.
Prints the sandbox command and runs nothing. It never writes a config file.
Writes or updates the project .ai-jail and exits.
Ignores the project .ai-jail for this run.
Generates permission configs for the AI tools themselves.
Shows the current .ai-jail configuration.
Shows every mount as the jail is built.

switches.layersLink: How it works explains what each layer does.
switches.more: Run ai-jail --help for the rest: the status bar, worktrees, mise and terminal options. The toolchains key is inverted like the older ones: no_toolchains = true turns them off.

secrets.title: Hide secrets inside the project
secrets.lede: Your .env file lives in the project, and the project is readable and writable. With the network on, the agent can send out whatever it can read there. Masking takes those files away.
secrets.alt: A project folder. The agent reaches src, package.json and README.md. The .env file is masked and the secrets folder is denied: both are dim and barred, and no line from the agent reaches them.
secrets.caption: The rest of the project stays as it was.

points.title: --mask <PATH|GLOB>
points.text: Replaces every match with an empty placeholder. The agent sees that the file exists and gets no content, so tools that only check for it keep working.

points.title: --deny-path <PATH|GLOB>
points.text: Makes every match a permission error.

points.title: --mask-except and --deny-path-except
points.text: Carve one path back out of a rule. They weaken protection, so a project file cannot set them.

secrets.flagsNote: # quote globs so ai-jail gets the pattern, not your shell's expansion
secrets.tomlNote: # a project file may tighten, so this works in the repository too

caveat.title: Only paths that exist at launch are covered
caveat.text: A path that is missing, or a glob that matches nothing, is skipped with a warning. A file created later, during the session, is not covered. If you need the rule enforced, create the file first. An empty .env is enough.

keys.title: Keep API keys out of every config file
keys.text: Masking covers files in the project. For the agent's own key, pass it from your shell with --env NAME, or from a file only you can read with --env-from-file. Neither is ever written to a .ai-jail file, and a project file cannot set them. With filtered egress on, --secret KEY=host also keeps the real value out of the sandbox; the recipe below shows it.
keys.shellNote: # the file must be yours, mode 0600 and outside the project
keys.tomlNote: # global file only; a project file that sets this is ignored

toolchains.title: Your toolchains come along
toolchains.lede: A build needs compilers, package managers and their caches. On Linux, ai-jail brings them in by default: the tools read only, the caches in a store the jail owns, and the package registries reachable through the filtered proxy.
toolchains.alt: Inside the jail wall, the agent reaches a locked toolbox labeled Toolchains and a box labeled Jail cache. Outside the wall, the host cache is dim and barred with no line to it. On the right, a line from the agent passes a gate and a proxy box to a cloud labeled Registries. Above it, the Model API cloud is dim and barred.
toolchains.caption: The host's own caches stay outside, so a jailed build cannot poison what the host builds from. The agent's API stays closed until you open it.

points.title: Tools, read only
points.text: Since 2.4.1, ai-jail maps mise installs and config read only. For Rust it maps ~/.cargo/bin and ~/.rustup the same way, so cargo and rustc resolve. Cargo's credentials and config.toml stay out. Because mise cannot install anything into a read-only map, ai-jail sets MISE_NOT_FOUND_AUTO_INSTALL=false inside, so a missing tool fails once instead of on every call.

points.title: A cache the jail owns
points.text: Dependency caches live under ~/.local/share/ai-jail/cache/ and survive between sessions. Cargo's registry and git caches go there. So does the default cache of pip, uv, Go, npm, yarn, pnpm, bun, deno, Maven, Gradle, Coursier, Composer, Crystal and Zig, when that tool's directory exists on your machine.

points.title: Registries, through the proxy
points.text: With toolchains on and no network flag given, the sandbox reaches crates.io, npm, PyPI, the Go proxy, Maven Central, Clojars, Packagist and github.com, each with its subdomains, through the same proxy as --allow-host, and nothing else. A known agent's own API host is allowed the same way, on macOS too; the registries are Linux only.

code.offline: # caches on, no network at all

optout.title: Turning it off
optout.text: --no-toolchains, or no_toolchains = true, turns off the caches and the registry default together. --no-network keeps the caches and closes the registries. Lockdown turns toolchains off, and a project file can only turn them off.

caveat.title: Two limits
caveat.text: cargo install to the global bin does not work inside the jail; use cargo install --root. The registry default needs an unprivileged network namespace. Where the kernel refuses one, the sandbox stays offline without saying so, while an explicit --allow-host still fails closed.

turnDown.title: Turning it down
turnDown.lede: The default is tuned for getting work done. Each step below closes one more thing, and --lockdown closes most of them at once. Security explains what each one protects against.

items.text: The default: the agent's login and its own API host, your toolchains on Linux, the package registries, and the project read and write.
--no-network: fully offline. Or an explicit --allow-host list, which replaces the default with only the hosts you name.
--no-agent-state: no login. The harness's state stays out and its API key is not copied.
--no-toolchains: no dependency caches and no package registries.
--mask, --deny-path and --hide-dotdir take single paths away, and a narrow --map or --rw-map replaces a broad grant.
--lockdown: the project read only, no login, no toolchains, no registries, strict Landlock and seccomp, and still not a VM.

other.title: One flag goes the other way
other.text: --no-private-home adds exposure: the agent gets your real home directory in place of the fresh one. For a single path, use --map or --rw-map instead.

lockdown.title: Lockdown: let an agent read code it must not change
lockdown.lede: --lockdown is for reviews and audits. The agent can read the project and answer questions about it, and it cannot change a file in it.
lockdown.alt: Two panels. In normal mode the agent sits inside the wall next to a project folder it can read and write, and a /tmp folder. In lockdown the wall is thicker, the project folder is read only, and /tmp is the only writable place.
lockdown.caption: The agent and project are the same, and only a temporary directory is writable.

items.text: The project is mounted read only
Only /tmp is writable on Linux. On macOS nothing is
No dot-directories from your home, no extra maps, no overlays
The environment is cleared and PATH is fixed to system directories
Landlock is mandatory: if it cannot be applied, the launch fails
Tighter limits on processes, open files and file size
No display, audio, GPU, KVM, Docker, SSH agent or mise, whatever else you passed
No toolchain caches, registry egress or tool credentials
No agent login, so the harness starts logged out

network.title: Lockdown and the network
network.text: Lockdown always isolates the network namespace, even when you pass --network. --allow-host still works under lockdown: the agent reaches the listed hosts through the proxy and nothing else.

recipes.title: Recipes
recipes.lede: Copy one. To see what it builds, run it with --dry-run first.

items.title: A cloud agent, day to day
items.text: Nothing to add. A known agent starts logged in and reaches its own API host through the filtered proxy, and nothing else. When a task needs more, put allow_hosts in the global file with the API host plus the extra ones, or open the whole network with network = true.

items.title: An agent ai-jail does not know
items.text: ai-jail allows the API host by itself for four agents: Claude api.anthropic.com, Codex api.openai.com, Gemini generativelanguage.googleapis.com and Grok api.x.ai. Any other agent gets its host from you with --allow-host. If the host is missing from the list, the launch warning names it.

items.title: A logged-out run
items.text: When the agent should have no credentials at all, --no-agent-state keeps its state directory and its API key out. It starts logged out, and whatever it logs into inside the fresh home is gone when the run ends.

items.title: Allowed hosts in the global file
items.text: The list applies to every run of that command, and it replaces the default, so keep the API host in it. An allowed host is trusted as a whole: github.com lets the agent push to any repository your credentials can reach, so add it only when you want that.

items.title: A key the agent never sees
items.text: The sandbox gets a placeholder in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and ai-jail's proxy puts the real key only into requests to api.anthropic.com. The client must send plain HTTP to the proxy for that host, which the http:// base URL does; ai-jail then carries the request to the real host over TLS. A client that only opens HTTPS tunnels keeps working, without substitution.

items.title: Git push over SSH
items.text: --ssh mounts ~/.ssh read only and forwards your SSH agent socket. Pushing also needs the network.

items.title: Build and test inside the jail
items.text: Nothing to add on Linux. cargo build, npm install or go get fetch from the registries through the proxy and cache into the jail's own store, and mise installs come along read only. For a run that touches nothing and reaches nothing, turn both off.

items.title: GitHub CLI inside the jail
items.text: --github mounts your gh config directory read only and forwards your active github.com token as GH_TOKEN, so gh is logged in, keyring or not. It reaches api.github.com through the default registry list, which covers github.com and its subdomains, so you add no host. Anything in the jail can then act on GitHub as you.

items.title: A browser for the agent
items.text: --browser alone gives a browser that cannot load a page or open a window. On Linux it also needs --network and --display, and an X11 browser needs --x11 in place of --display.

items.title: Separate Claude profiles
items.text: Keep work and personal logins apart by pointing each run at its own Claude directory.

items.title: Try a risky refactor on a copy
items.text: An overlay keeps the agent's writes in a side layer under .ai-jail-overlays in the project. Compare it with the original afterward and keep what you like. Linux only.

comments.nothing: # nothing to add: login and api.anthropic.com come by default
comments.more: # when a task needs more, once in ~/.ai-jail (the list replaces the default)
comments.open: # or open the whole network: network = true
comments.hosts: # claude, codex, gemini and grok need no flag: ai-jail allows their API host by itself
comments.phantom: # the key lives in the 0600 file; the sandbox only ever sees AIJAIL-PHANTOM-...
comments.build: # default on Linux: caches on, registries reachable through the proxy

compat.title: Old configs keep working
compat.text: Backward compatibility is a project rule: the project never removes a flag or a config key. Unknown keys are ignored and missing ones take their defaults, so a file written for an old version still loads.
compat.legacy: Older switches keep their inverted names, where true turns the thing off: no_gpu, no_docker, no_display, no_mise, no_toolchains, no_landlock, no_seccomp, no_rlimits. That is why --gpu is saved as no_gpu = false. Newer switches use plain names such as network = true. --allow-tcp-port is still parsed and still refuses to launch, because it cannot fence UDP. Its error points at --allow-host.
